title: Raspberry Mousse
subtitle: Fresh raspberry purée, lightly set with cream and a little gelatine
excerpt: Bright, sharp raspberry purée folded through whipped cream and lightened with egg whites. The colour is vivid pink; the flavour is clean and fruity. Chill for 2 hours.
sourceNotes: Raspberry mousse has appeared in British dessert cooking since at least the Edwardian era, when fruit-based creams and mousses were a fixture of formal dining. The modern version, combining fruit purée with whipped cream and gelatine, is a simplified descendant of the classic bavarois.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to a day ahead and keep covered in the fridge.

content.text: Raspberry mousse is a light, fruit-forward dessert built from fresh raspberry purée, softly whipped cream, and, for extra airiness, stiffly beaten egg whites folded through at the end. The result is a vivid deep-pink mousse with a clean, sharp fruit flavour and a texture that is light enough to feel barely substantial, despite the cream. Sieve the purée to remove the seeds before folding, the seeds are edible, but the smooth version is noticeably more elegant.
Blend the raspberries with half the caster sugar and the lemon juice until smooth. Press through a fine sieve into a bowl, discarding the seeds. You should have about 250ml of smooth purée.

Soak the gelatine leaves in cold water for 5 minutes. Warm 3 tablespoons of the raspberry purée in a small saucepan over a low heat until just steaming. Squeeze the gelatine dry and stir into the warm purée until fully dissolved. Pour the gelatine purée back into the main purée and stir together. Leave to cool until barely warm.

Whip the double cream to soft peaks in a large bowl. Fold the cooled raspberry purée into the cream in two additions. If using egg whites, whisk them with the remaining caster sugar to firm, glossy peaks in a clean bowl, then fold through the raspberry cream in two stages. Spoon into glasses or ramekins and refrigerate for at least 2 hours until lightly set.

items.cause: The purée was not sieved thoroughly enough to remove all the seeds.
items.fix: Use a fine-mesh sieve and press the purée through with the back of a spoon. Work in batches if needed, it takes a minute or two to get all the juice through.

items.cause: Raspberries vary in acidity depending on how ripe they are.
items.fix: Add an extra tablespoon of caster sugar to the purée before sieving and taste before folding into the cream.

items.symptom: Mousse did not set and is runny
items.cause: The gelatine may not have fully dissolved, or the purée was still warm when folded into the cream.
items.fix: Allow the gelatine purée to cool until barely warm before folding into the whipped cream, a warm purée will collapse the cream. Ensure the gelatine was completely dissolved and no strands remain.

content.text: Best eaten on the day. Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 2 days; the texture softens slightly but remains good. Do not freeze.
